# About this tutorial

This tutorial analyses a complete pooled shRNA screen with ScreenR, from the
raw barcode counts to a list of genes whose knockdown is depleted **because
of the treatment**, and to the evidence that supports each of them. The
screen has the structure of many drug-sensitization screens: an infected and
selected cell population is split into control and treated cultures, which
are sampled at two time points with three biological replicates each.

The question is not only "which genes are depleted?", but:

* Which genes are depleted in **treated cells compared with control cells
  at the same time point**, rather than lost in all cultures because they are
  needed for growth (essential genes)?
* Is the depletion supported by **several shRNAs** of the gene and by the
  **biological replicates**?
* Is it present at **both time points**, or does it appear (or grow) over
  time?

Each step explains why it is needed, what ScreenR does, how to read the
result and which decisions it involves. The tutorials
[1](Tutorial_1_Creating_the_object.html),
[2](Tutorial_2_Quality_control.html) and
[3](Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.html) describe the individual functions in more
detail; this one puts them together for a longitudinal design.

```{r packages, warning = FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
```

ScreenR does not impose a look on its plots: they use the current ggplot2
theme, so a theme set once with `theme_set()` applies to every plot of the
analysis. Here we use a light theme with slightly larger text:

```{r theme}
theme_set(theme_light(base_size = 12))
```

# The experiment

## Design

The cells are infected with a pooled library of barcoded shRNAs (about 10
shRNAs for each of 534 genes) and selected with puromycin, which kills the
cells that were not infected. The selected population is then split into
control and treated cultures, sampled at two time points:

| Sample(s) | Stage | Condition | Replicates | Role in the analysis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T0 | Right after infection, before selection | Infected cells | 1 | Representation of the library in the cells; quality control of the infection |
| Puro | After puromycin selection | Baseline | 1 | Starting population of all the cultures; reference for the loss of fitness |
| T3 | First time point | Control | 3 | Reference for the treatment effect at T3 |
| T3 | First time point | Treated | 3 | Treatment effect at T3 |
| T4 | Second time point | Control | 3 | Reference for the treatment effect at T4 |
| T4 | Second time point | Treated | 3 | Treatment effect at T4 |

That is 14 samples. The controls and the treated cultures have the same
history except the treatment, so **the treatment effect is measured as treated
versus control at the same time point**: whatever happens in both (for
example the loss of shRNAs against genes needed for growth) cancels out. The
T0 and Puro samples are single references: they describe where the cultures
start from and are used for quality control and for the fitness effects, not
for the treatment effect.

```{r design-figure, fig.height = 3.2, echo = FALSE}
stages <- c("T0", "Puro", "T3", "T4")
conditions <- c("Treated", "Control", "Baseline", "Infected")
design_plot <- tibble(
    Stage = c("T0", "Puro", "T3", "T3", "T4", "T4"),
    Condition = c("Infected", "Baseline", "Control", "Treated", "Control",
        "Treated"),
    Replicates = c(1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 3)
) %>%
    mutate(x = match(Stage, stages), y = match(Condition, conditions))
links <- tibble(
    from = c("T0", "Puro", "Puro", "T3", "T3"),
    to = c("Puro", "T3", "T3", "T4", "T4"),
    from_condition = c("Infected", "Baseline", "Baseline", "Control",
        "Treated"),
    to_condition = c("Baseline", "Control", "Treated", "Control", "Treated")
)
ggplot(design_plot, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_segment(data = links, aes(
        x = match(from, stages) + 0.15, xend = match(to, stages) - 0.15,
        y = match(from_condition, conditions),
        yend = match(to_condition, conditions)
    ), arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), colour = "grey50") +
    geom_label(aes(label = paste0("n = ", Replicates), fill = Condition),
        show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Treated = "#D95F02", Control = "#1B9E77",
        Baseline = "#999999", Infected = "#CCCCCC")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(stages), labels = stages,
        expand = expansion(add = 0.4)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq_along(conditions), labels = conditions,
        expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
    labs(x = "Stage of the screen", y = NULL,
        title = "Experimental design (n = biological replicates)")
```

## The data

ScreenR includes this screen as `count_table` (the reads of each barcode in
each sample, from the alignment of the sequencing reads to the library) and
`annotation_table` (the gene targeted by each barcode). See
`?count_table` and `?annotation_table`.

```{r data}
data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)
dim(count_table)
colnames(count_table)
head(annotation_table[, c("Barcode", "Gene")], 3)
```

The count table has three rows with the barcode `"*"`: the reads that could
not be assigned to any shRNA. They are not barcodes and appear several times,
so they are removed. ScreenR would refuse duplicated barcode identifiers
rather than guess how to combine them (`duplicate_barcodes` can sum them
instead).

```{r unmapped}
table(count_table$Barcode == "*")
counts <- count_table[count_table$Barcode != "*", ]
```

The original sample names are not self-explanatory, so the samples are
renamed, and their stage, condition and replicate are described explicitly in
a sample table instead of being parsed from the names:

```{r sample-table}
samples <- tibble(
    Original = colnames(counts)[-1],
    Sample = c("T0_Infected", "Puro_Baseline",
        paste0("T3_TRT_", 1:3), paste0("T3_CTRL_", 1:3),
        paste0("T4_TRT_", 1:3), paste0("T4_CTRL_", 1:3)),
    Day = c("T0", "Puro", rep("T3", 6), rep("T4", 6)),
    Treatment = c("Infected", "Baseline", rep(c("TRT", "CTRL"), each = 3),
        rep(c("TRT", "CTRL"), each = 3)),
    Replicate = c(NA, NA, rep(1:3, 4))
)
samples$Group <- ifelse(samples$Day %in% c("T0", "Puro"), samples$Day,
    paste(samples$Day, samples$Treatment, sep = "_"))
knitr::kable(samples)
colnames(counts) <- c("Barcode", samples$Sample)
```

The **groups** define the statistical model: one group for each combination
of time point and condition (and one for each reference sample). Replicates
of the same group are what the model uses to measure the biological
variability.

# The ScreenR object

## Colors that mean the same thing in every plot

When the object is created, a palette can be given for each sample variable
(Treatment, Group, Day, Sample, ...). Every plot of ScreenR that colors the
samples by one of these variables then uses it, so that, for example, the
treated cultures have the same color in all the figures. Here the controls
are green and the treated cultures orange, darker at the later time point,
and the two reference samples are grey:

```{r palettes}
group_colors <- c(T0 = "#CCCCCC", Puro = "#999999",
    T3_CTRL = "#66C2A5", T3_TRT = "#FC8D62",
    T4_CTRL = "#1B9E77", T4_TRT = "#D95F02")
palettes <- list(
    Treatment = c(Infected = "#CCCCCC", Baseline = "#999999",
        CTRL = "#1B9E77", TRT = "#D95F02"),
    Group = group_colors,
    Day = c(T0 = "#CCCCCC", Puro = "#999999", T3 = "#7570B3",
        T4 = "#E7298A"),
    # Each sample takes the color of its group
    Sample = setNames(group_colors[samples$Group], samples$Sample)
)
```

## Creating the object

```{r object}
object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts,
    annotation = annotation_table,
    groups = factor(samples$Group,
        levels = c("T0", "Puro", "T3_CTRL", "T3_TRT", "T4_CTRL", "T4_TRT")),
    sample_table = samples[, c("Sample", "Day", "Treatment")],
    replicates = samples$Replicate,
    palettes = palettes
)
object
names(get_palettes(object))
```

The palettes are checked when they are set (every value of the variable must
have a color) and can be changed later with `set_palettes()`. A palette given
directly to a plot replaces the one of the object.

The ScreenR object is a `SummarizedExperiment`, the standard Bioconductor
container for assays with row and column annotation. Each piece of
information is stored once, in the place that fits it:

* `assay(object, "counts")`: the raw counts only, one row per barcode and one
  column per sample. The barcode identifiers are the row names (as text), not
  a column of the counts.
* `rowData(object)`: the annotation of each barcode (its gene), aligned with
  the rows.
* `colData(object)`: the Day, Treatment, Group and Replicate of each sample,
  aligned with the columns.

```{r se-parts}
assay(object, "counts")[1:3, 1:4]
rowData(object)[1:3, c("Barcode", "Gene")]
colData(object)[c(1, 2, 3, 9), c("Day", "Treatment", "Group", "Replicate")]
```

Because rows and columns are matched by identifier, subsetting or reordering
the object keeps counts, annotation and sample information together, and the
object can be used with any Bioconductor tool that accepts a
`SummarizedExperiment`. The barcodes with no read in any sample carry no
information and are removed:

```{r zero-rows}
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
dim(object)
```

# Quality control

Before looking for hits, we check that the screen worked: enough reads in
every sample, a library that is still well represented, and replicates that
agree. These checks use the raw counts, except where noted.

## Sequencing depth

Each sample should have many more reads than barcodes, so that the counts of
each shRNA are not dominated by sampling noise.

```{r depth, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_mapped_reads(object) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

```{r depth-numbers}
depth <- mapped_reads(object)
range(depth$Mapped) / nrow(object)
```

Every sample has between `r round(min(depth$Mapped) / nrow(object))` and
`r round(max(depth$Mapped) / nrow(object))` reads per barcode on average,
well above the usual minimum of a few hundred.

## Library representation over the screen

Infection and puromycin selection are bottlenecks: shRNAs carried by few
cells can be lost by chance, independently of their target. The number of
barcodes without any read and the Gini index (how unevenly the reads are
spread over the barcodes: 0 when even, close to 1 when a few barcodes take
most reads) show how the representation evolves.

```{r representation, fig.height = 6}
(plot_barcode_lost(object) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))) /
    plot_gini(object)
```

Few barcodes are lost at T0 and after selection, and the Gini index increases
slowly over time, as expected when the shRNAs against genes needed for growth
drop out. Neither the infection nor the selection caused a bottleneck that
would make the counts unreliable.

## Agreement between replicates

The replicates of a condition should be more similar to each other than to
the other samples. This and the following plots compare **normalized**
counts, so the counts are normalized first, with the TMM method (see the
next section).

```{r normalize-for-qc}
object <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")
```

```{r replicates, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 7}
plot_replicate_correlation(object)
```

```{r replicate-correlation}
correlation <- cor(log2(get_normalized_count_table(object)[, -1] + 1))
round(correlation["T4_TRT_1", c("T4_TRT_2", "T4_TRT_3", "T3_CTRL_2",
    "T3_TRT_1")], 3)
```

All the correlations are high, and the T3 samples are more similar to each
other than to the T4 samples. One sample stands out: **T4_TRT_1** is more
correlated with some T3 samples (for example T3_CTRL_2) than with the other
two T4 treated replicates, and it lost far fewer barcodes than them (see
above). Removing a replicate needs a technical reason, which we do not have,
so it is kept; the [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity) at the end checks that
the conclusions do not depend on it.

## Structure of the samples

Multidimensional scaling (MDS) and principal component analysis (PCA) place
similar samples close to each other.

```{r mds, fig.height = 4}
plot_mds(object)
plot_pca(object)
```

The first dimension orders the samples by time (T0 and Puro, then T3, then
T4): the largest source of variation is the growth of the cells, which
changes the representation of the shRNAs against growth genes in all the
cultures. This is why the treatment effect must be measured **within each
time point**. At T3 the treated and control samples overlap. At T4 two treated
replicates (T4_TRT_2 and T4_TRT_3) move away from the controls, in different
directions on the second dimension, while T4_TRT_1 stays with the controls:
the treated cultures at T4 are heterogeneous, which limits the power to
detect treatment effects.

# Normalization

Samples are sequenced at different depths, so counts are compared after
dividing each sample by an **effective library size**. This analysis uses the
**TMM** normalization of edgeR (`normalize_data(method = "tmm")`): the
effective library size of a sample is its total number of reads multiplied by
a TMM factor, which corrects the total when many barcodes are depleted or
enriched in some samples, as happens over the growth of the cultures and with
the treatment.

```{r normalization}
normalization <- get_normalization(object)
normalization$method
round(normalization$norm_factors, 3)
```

The TMM factors stay close to 1, but they differ between the time points:
the factors correct the totals for the shRNAs that drop out over time.

**One normalization for the whole analysis.** ScreenR records the
normalization in the object (the effective library sizes in the colData, the
method and the TMM factors in the metadata) and never changes the raw counts.
Every result below uses this same normalization: the normalized counts of the
plots, the descriptive fold changes and the statistical models. The models use
the raw counts, as negative binomial models require, with the effective
library sizes as offsets, so the TMM factors are applied once:

```{r one-normalization}
dge <- create_edger_obj(object)
all.equal(dge$samples$lib.size * dge$samples$norm.factors,
    unname(normalization$effective_library_size))
```

Changing the normalization with `normalize_data()` would update all of them
at once.

# The statistical model

## Why a model with all the samples

The treatment effect of a gene could be measured with fold changes of mean
counts, but this ignores two essential sources of information: the
**replicates**, which tell how much a fold change varies between independent
cultures, and the **several shRNAs** of each gene, whose agreement makes a
hit credible. ScreenR therefore models the raw counts of each barcode with
the negative binomial generalized linear model of edgeR, and then tests the
barcodes of each gene together.

The model has one coefficient for each group (the mean abundance of the
barcode in that group), and every comparison is a **contrast**, a combination
of group coefficients. All 14 samples enter the same model, so the
variability between replicates is estimated from all the replicated groups at
once.

```{r design}
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
colnames(design)
```

## The comparisons

The questions of the screen are contrasts between these groups:

```{r contrasts}
contrasts <- list(
    # Treatment effect at each time point: treated vs control
    T3 = create_contrast(design, treatment = "T3_TRT", control = "T3_CTRL"),
    T4 = create_contrast(design, treatment = "T4_TRT", control = "T4_CTRL"),
    # Average treatment effect over the two time points
    Average = create_contrast(design,
        treatment = c("T3_TRT", "T4_TRT"), control = c("T3_CTRL", "T4_CTRL")),
    # Loss of fitness: T4 vs the post-selection baseline, in each condition
    Fitness_CTRL = create_contrast(design, treatment = "T4_CTRL",
        control = "Puro"),
    Fitness_TRT = create_contrast(design, treatment = "T4_TRT",
        control = "Puro")
)
contrasts$T4
```

A gene that is lost in all the cultures because it is needed for growth has
a strong fitness effect in both conditions but no treatment effect, because
treated and control cultures lose it in the same way. A treatment-specific
hit has a treatment effect: it is depleted in treated cultures **compared
with the controls of the same time point**.

## Gene-level test

For each contrast, `find_roast_hit(method = "fry")` tests whether the
barcodes of a gene, taken together, are depleted. FRY is a fast,
self-contained gene-set test of limma: it uses the replicate variability of
the edgeR model and all the shRNAs of the gene, so a gene is called when its
shRNAs are depleted consistently, relative to the variability between
replicates. Its `Log2FC` is the median log2 fold change of the shRNAs of the
gene. In the screens with known hits of the
[benchmark](Benchmark_MAGeCK.html) and of
[Tutorial 4](Tutorial_4_CRISPR_screens.html), FRY found most of the
essential genes with few false calls.

The function returns one-sided p-values for the requested direction. To
combine contrasts, we want the p-value of depletion for **every** gene, so
this small helper also converts the genes that change in the other direction
(their p-value of depletion is one minus their p-value of enrichment):

```{r gene-test}
gene_test <- function(contrast) {
    down <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast,
        method = "fry", direction = "Down", fdr = 1)
    up <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast,
        method = "fry", direction = "Up", fdr = 1)
    bind_rows(
        transmute(down, Gene, NBarcodes = NGenes, Log2FC, PValue),
        transmute(up, Gene, NBarcodes = NGenes, Log2FC, PValue = 1 - PValue)
    ) %>%
        mutate(FDR = p.adjust(PValue, method = "BH")) %>%
        arrange(PValue)
}
tests <- lapply(contrasts, gene_test)
head(tests$T4)
```

The FDR column corrects for testing all the genes (Benjamini-Hochberg): a
gene with FDR at most 0.05 is a hit, and on average at most 5% of the hits
are false.

```{r hits-per-contrast}
sapply(tests, function(result) c(
    `FDR <= 0.05` = sum(result$FDR <= 0.05),
    `FDR <= 0.10` = sum(result$FDR <= 0.10)
))
```

## How much signal is there?

Before reading the lists of hits, the distribution of the p-values tells how
many genes respond at all. Without any effect, the two-sided p-values (for a
change in either direction) are uniform between 0 and 1; genes with an effect
add an excess of small p-values.

```{r p-value-histogram, fig.height = 3.5}
two_sided <- function(result) 2 * pmin(result$PValue, 1 - result$PValue)
bind_rows(lapply(tests[c("T3", "T4", "Average")],
    function(result) tibble(PValue = two_sided(result))), .id = "Contrast") %>%
    ggplot(aes(PValue)) +
    geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), colour = "white") +
    facet_wrap(~Contrast) +
    labs(x = "Two-sided p-value (FRY)", y = "Genes")
```

The share of genes with an effect can be estimated as one minus the share of
uniform p-values (estimated from the p-values above 0.5):

```{r pi0}
with_effect <- function(result) {
    1 - min(1, mean(two_sided(result) > 0.5) / 0.5)
}
round(sapply(tests[c("T3", "T4", "Average")], with_effect), 2)
```

About `r round(100 * with_effect(tests$T3))`% of the genes respond to the
treatment at T3 and `r round(100 * with_effect(tests$T4))`% at T4: **at T3
there is no detectable treatment effect**, while at T4 a group of genes
changes. The same is visible in the distribution of the barcode log2 fold
changes (treated vs control), which is wider at T4. The tables of
`compute_metrics()` do not carry the palettes of the object, so the Day
palette is given to the plot:

```{r zscore-distribution, fig.height = 3.5}
metrics <- list(
    T3 = compute_metrics(object, control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT",
        day = "T3"),
    T4 = compute_metrics(object, control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT",
        day = "T4")
)
plot_zscore_distribution(metrics, alpha = 0.5,
    palette = get_palettes(object)$Day)
```

# Treatment-specific hits

## At each time point, with several methods

```{r time-point-hits}
hits_t3 <- filter(tests$T3, FDR <= 0.05)
hits_t4 <- filter(tests$T4, FDR <= 0.05)
hits_t4
```

At 5% FDR, FRY finds `r nrow(hits_t3)` depleted genes at T3 and
`r nrow(hits_t4)` at T4.

ScreenR has other gene-level tests, which look at the same barcodes with
different assumptions. Running them all on the same contrasts tells how much
a hit depends on the choice of the method:

* **FRY** and **ROAST** (`find_roast_hit()`) are *self-contained* tests:
  are the shRNAs of the gene depleted, relative to the variability between
  replicates? ROAST computes its p-values by random rotations, FRY with a
  fast approximation of them.
* **CAMERA** (`find_camera_hit()`) is a *competitive* test: is the gene more
  depleted than the other genes of the library, allowing for the correlation
  between the shRNAs of a gene?
* The **gene-level Z-score test** (`find_gene_zscore_hit()`) compares the mean
  Z-score of the shRNAs of a gene with a null distribution: random sets of
  barcodes (the default) or an empirical null estimated from all the genes
  (see [Choosing the reference of the gene-level test](Empirical_null.html)).
  The Z-scores come from `compute_barcode_statistics()`, which tests every
  barcode with the same edgeR model, so they include the replicate
  variability. It is also a competitive test.

```{r all-methods}
run_methods <- function(contrast) {
    statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(object, design, contrast)
    list(
        FRY = find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast, method = "fry",
            direction = "Down", fdr = 1),
        ROAST = find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast, method = "roast",
            nrot = 9999, seed = 1, direction = "Down", fdr = 1),
        CAMERA = find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast,
            direction = "Down", fdr = 1),
        `Z-score, empirical null` = find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
            reference = "empirical", fdr = 1),
        `Z-score, random barcodes` = find_gene_zscore_hit(statistics,
            n_permutations = 1e5, seed = 1, fdr = 1)
    )
}
methods_t3 <- run_methods(contrasts$T3)
methods_t4 <- run_methods(contrasts$T4)
sapply(list(T3 = methods_t3, T4 = methods_t4), function(results) {
    sapply(results, function(result) sum(result$FDR <= 0.05))
})
```

`plot_common_hit()` shows how the hits of the methods overlap. With more than
three methods it draws an UpSet plot: each column is a combination of methods
(the dots below), and its bar counts the genes found by exactly those
methods; the bars on the left are the hits of each method.

```{r upset-t4, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_common_hit(methods_t4, fdr = 0.05,
    title = "Depleted genes at T4 (5% FDR)")
```

At T4 the two self-contained tests agree exactly, while the competitive tests
find no gene at 5% FDR. At a looser threshold the overlap shows which genes
come closest to the competitive tests as well:

```{r upset-t4-relaxed, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_common_hit(methods_t4, fdr = 0.25,
    title = "Depleted genes at T4 (25% FDR)")
```

At T3 no method finds any depleted gene:

```{r upset-t3, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_common_hit(methods_t3, fdr = 0.05,
    title = "Depleted genes at T3 (5% FDR)")
```

`summarise_hits()` puts the FDR of every method in one table:

```{r method-agreement}
agreement <- summarise_hits(methods_t4, fdr = 0.05)
agreement %>%
    filter(Gene %in% hits_t4$Gene) %>%
    select(Gene, NMethods, starts_with("FDR")) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The two kinds of tests ask different questions. FRY and ROAST call a gene
when its shRNAs are depleted more than the replicates vary; CAMERA and the
Z-score tests call it only when it is more depleted than the other genes of
the library. The effects at T4 are moderate (median log2 fold changes
between `r round(min(hits_t4$Log2FC), 2)` and
`r round(max(hits_t4$Log2FC), 2)`): they are reproducible depletions, but they
do not stand out against all the other genes. These are **candidates with
moderate effects**; the next sections collect the evidence needed to choose
which of them to validate.

## Across the two time points: three different questions

"Consistently depleted over time" can mean three different things, which need
three different tests. Being significant at T3 and, separately, at T4 answers
none of them exactly.

1. **Is the gene depleted at T3 and at T4?** This is tested by the
   *intersection-union test*: the gene is called only if both one-sided
   tests reject, so its p-value is the larger of the two
   (p = max(p<sub>T3</sub>, p<sub>T4</sub>)), corrected for the number of
   genes. It is the formal test of reproducibility across time points.
2. **Is the gene depleted on average over the two time points?** The
   `Average` contrast tests the mean of the two treatment effects. It can be
   significant because of one time point only.
3. **Does the treatment effect change between T3 and T4?** This is the
   interaction, (T4 treated - T4 control) - (T3 treated - T3 control), tested
   by `find_time_hit()` (next section).

```{r intersection-union}
genes <- tests$T3$Gene
both <- tibble(
    Gene = genes,
    Log2FC_T3 = tests$T3$Log2FC[match(genes, tests$T3$Gene)],
    Log2FC_T4 = tests$T4$Log2FC[match(genes, tests$T4$Gene)],
    P_T3 = tests$T3$PValue[match(genes, tests$T3$Gene)],
    P_T4 = tests$T4$PValue[match(genes, tests$T4$Gene)]
) %>%
    mutate(
        PValue_both = pmax(P_T3, P_T4),
        FDR_both = p.adjust(PValue_both, method = "BH"),
        FDR_average = tests$Average$FDR[match(Gene, tests$Average$Gene)]
    ) %>%
    arrange(PValue_both)
head(both, 5)
```

```{r consistency-summary}
c(
    `depleted at T3 and at T4 (intersection-union)` =
        sum(both$FDR_both <= 0.05),
    `depleted on average` = sum(both$FDR_average <= 0.05),
    `depleted at T4` = nrow(hits_t4)
)
```

No gene is depleted at both time points, and the average effect identifies
`r sum(both$FDR_average <= 0.05)` gene(s): the average is diluted by the T3
effects, which are close to zero. In this screen **the treatment-specific
depletion appears at T4**; it is not a constant effect present from T3.

## Does the effect change over time?

`find_time_hit()` fits a single model to the control and treated samples of
the two time points, with a separate line for each condition, and tests the
difference between their slopes, the change of the treatment effect from T3
to T4, with CAMERA. With two time points this is the interaction defined
above. It uses only the samples of the given days, so its variance estimates
differ slightly from those of the model with all the samples.

```{r time-hits}
time_hits <- find_time_hit(object, treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    days = c("T3", "T4"), direction = "Down", fdr = 1)
head(time_hits)
sum(time_hits$FDR <= 0.05)
```

```{r time-hits-t4}
time_hits %>%
    filter(Gene %in% hits_t4$Gene) %>%
    select(Gene, Log2FC, PValue, FDR)
```

By default `find_time_hit()` numbers the time points 0, 1, 2, ..., as if
they were equally spaced. With the real times (here we assume 7 and 14 days
after the end of the selection, the usual schedule of this protocol), the
`Log2FC` column becomes the change of the treatment effect per day. With two
time points the model is saturated, so the p-values do not change; with
three or more time points that are not equally spaced, the real times fit
the change of the treatment effect against the actual time and do change the
results.

```{r time-hits-days}
time_hits_days <- find_time_hit(object, treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    days = c("T3", "T4"), time = c(T3 = 7, T4 = 14), direction = "Down",
    fdr = 1)
same_genes <- match(time_hits$Gene, time_hits_days$Gene)
all.equal(time_hits_days$PValue[same_genes], time_hits$PValue)
head(select(time_hits_days, Gene, Log2FC, PValue))
```

No gene passes the FDR threshold. `r sum(time_hits$PValue[time_hits$Gene %in% hits_t4$Gene] < 0.01)`
of the `r nrow(hits_t4)` T4 hits have p-values below 0.01 for a stronger
depletion at T4 than at T3, which agrees with an effect that develops over
time, but this is not significant after correcting for the number of genes.
A non-significant interaction is **not**
evidence that the effect is the same at the two time points: it only means
that a change could not be demonstrated with three replicates. Showing that
two effects are equal would need an equivalence test, which ScreenR does not
provide (see [Limitations](#limitations)).

# Essential genes: loss of fitness in all the cultures

Some genes are depleted in every culture, treated or not, because the cells
need them to grow. They are found with the fitness contrasts (T4 against the
post-selection baseline) in each condition.

```{r fitness}
fitness <- tibble(Gene = genes) %>%
    mutate(
        Log2FC_CTRL = tests$Fitness_CTRL$Log2FC[
            match(Gene, tests$Fitness_CTRL$Gene)],
        FDR_CTRL = tests$Fitness_CTRL$FDR[
            match(Gene, tests$Fitness_CTRL$Gene)],
        Log2FC_TRT = tests$Fitness_TRT$Log2FC[
            match(Gene, tests$Fitness_TRT$Gene)],
        FDR_TRT = tests$Fitness_TRT$FDR[match(Gene, tests$Fitness_TRT$Gene)],
        FDR_treatment = tests$T4$FDR[match(Gene, tests$T4$Gene)]
    )
essential <- fitness %>%
    filter(FDR_CTRL <= 0.05, FDR_TRT <= 0.05, FDR_treatment > 0.05) %>%
    arrange(Log2FC_CTRL)
nrow(essential)
head(essential, 5)
```

`r nrow(essential)` genes are depleted in both conditions with no
significant treatment effect: they behave like essential genes. They are not
treatment-specific hits, even though they are among the most depleted genes of
the screen. For the two most depleted ones the treated cultures lose slightly
more than the controls at T4 (see the figure below), but this treatment effect
is not significant. The baseline has a single sample, so these contrasts rely
on the variability estimated from the replicated groups.

# Classification of the genes

Each gene gets one class, from the tests above:

```{r classification}
classes <- both %>%
    left_join(select(fitness, Gene, FDR_CTRL, FDR_TRT), by = "Gene") %>%
    mutate(
        FDR_T3 = tests$T3$FDR[match(Gene, tests$T3$Gene)],
        FDR_T4 = tests$T4$FDR[match(Gene, tests$T4$Gene)],
        Class = case_when(
            FDR_both <= 0.05 ~ "Treatment: T3 and T4",
            FDR_T4 <= 0.05 ~ "Treatment: T4",
            FDR_T3 <= 0.05 ~ "Treatment: T3",
            FDR_CTRL <= 0.05 & FDR_TRT <= 0.05 ~ "Fitness (both conditions)",
            TRUE ~ "Not significant"
        )
    )
dplyr::count(classes, Class)
```

The figure that summarizes the screen compares the treatment effect of each
gene at T3 and at T4. Genes depleted at both time points would lie in the
lower left quadrant, near the diagonal; genes whose effect appears at T4 lie
below zero on the vertical axis only.

```{r effect-map, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 7}
colours <- c(
    "Treatment: T3 and T4" = "#D95F02", "Treatment: T4" = "#E7298A",
    "Treatment: T3" = "#7570B3", "Fitness (both conditions)" = "#1B9E77",
    "Not significant" = "grey75"
)
# Label the treatment hits and the two most depleted fitness genes
labelled <- filter(classes, startsWith(Class, "Treatment") |
    Gene %in% essential$Gene[1:2])
ggplot(arrange(classes, Class != "Not significant"),
    aes(Log2FC_T3, Log2FC_T4, colour = Class)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
    geom_point(size = 1.8) +
    geom_text(data = labelled, aes(label = Gene), size = 2.6,
        vjust = -0.8, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = colours, drop = FALSE) +
    labs(
        x = "Treatment effect at T3 (median log2 fold change, TRT vs CTRL)",
        y = "Treatment effect at T4 (median log2 fold change, TRT vs CTRL)",
        colour = NULL
    ) +
    coord_equal()
```

The treatment-specific hits are depleted at T4 (negative vertical axis) with
small or no effects at T3 (horizontal axis): they lie away from the diagonal,
because their depletion appears between the two time points. Most fitness
genes have small treatment effects: they are lost in treated and control
cultures alike, so treated and control samples of the same time point differ
little even though both are strongly depleted over time.

# From candidates to the hits to validate

A gene-level FDR is the starting point, not the end of the analysis. Before
spending time on validation, each candidate is checked against the questions
that make a hit credible:

1. **Is it found by more than one method?** Here: FRY and ROAST, the two
   self-contained tests, both at 5% FDR.
2. **Is it supported by several shRNAs?** The number of shRNAs of the gene
   that are depleted on their own (barcode p-value below 0.05 in
   `compute_barcode_statistics()`), and the number of shRNAs that behave very
   differently from the others of the gene (`find_discordant_barcodes()`),
   which may point to off-target effects.
3. **Does it depend on a single sample?** The FRY FDR without T4_TRT_1, the
   treated replicate that resembles the controls.
4. **Is it treatment-specific?** Whether the gene is also lost in the control
   cultures (fitness contrast against the baseline): then the treatment
   enhances a loss of fitness rather than creating a new dependency.
5. **How does it behave over time?** Its effect at T3 and the p-value of the
   interaction, a stronger depletion at T4 than at T3.

## Sensitivity to one replicate {#sensitivity}

```{r sensitivity}
without <- object[, colnames(object) != "T4_TRT_1"]
design_without <- create_design_matrix(without)
t4_without <- find_roast_hit(without, design_without,
    create_contrast(design_without, "T4_TRT", "T4_CTRL"),
    method = "fry", direction = "Down", fdr = 1)
c(`T4 hits without T4_TRT_1` = sum(t4_without$FDR <= 0.05),
    `of which also hits with all the samples` =
        sum(t4_without$Gene[t4_without$FDR <= 0.05] %in% hits_t4$Gene))
```

Without T4_TRT_1, `r sum(t4_without$FDR <= 0.05)` genes pass 5% FDR at T4,
`r sum(t4_without$Gene[t4_without$FDR <= 0.05] %in% hits_t4$Gene)` of them
among the `r nrow(hits_t4)` hits found with all the samples, and
`r sum(t4_without$FDR[match(hits_t4$Gene, t4_without$Gene)] <= 0.10)` of these
`r nrow(hits_t4)` hits keep an FDR of at most 10%. With one treated replicate
fewer at T4 the test has less power: most hits fall just above the threshold
rather than disappearing. The direction of the evidence does not depend on
this replicate, but its strength does, which is one more reason to validate
the hits independently. (The subset keeps the normalization of the full
object: its samples keep their effective library sizes.)

## The evidence for each candidate

```{r evidence}
statistics_t4 <- compute_barcode_statistics(object, design, contrasts$T4)
discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics$T4, threshold = 3)
fdr_of <- function(result, genes) result$FDR[match(genes, result$Gene)]
evidence <- tibble(Gene = hits_t4$Gene) %>%
    mutate(
        Log2FC_T4 = tests$T4$Log2FC[match(Gene, tests$T4$Gene)],
        Log2FC_T3 = tests$T3$Log2FC[match(Gene, tests$T3$Gene)],
        FDR_FRY = fdr_of(methods_t4$FRY, Gene),
        FDR_ROAST = fdr_of(methods_t4$ROAST, Gene),
        FDR_CAMERA = fdr_of(methods_t4$CAMERA, Gene),
        shRNAs = vapply(Gene, function(gene) {
            sum(statistics_t4$Gene == gene)
        }, integer(1)),
        Depleted_shRNAs = vapply(Gene, function(gene) {
            sum(statistics_t4$Gene == gene & statistics_t4$Log2FC < 0 &
                statistics_t4$PValue < 0.05)
        }, integer(1)),
        Discordant_shRNAs = vapply(Gene, function(gene) {
            sum(discordant$Gene == gene)
        }, integer(1)),
        FDR_without_T4_TRT_1 = fdr_of(t4_without, Gene),
        FDR_fitness_CTRL = tests$Fitness_CTRL$FDR[
            match(Gene, tests$Fitness_CTRL$Gene)],
        P_interaction = time_hits$PValue[match(Gene, time_hits$Gene)]
    )
```

The candidates are ranked with explicit rules, written once in the code so
that they can be read, discussed and changed:

* **Priority 1**: found by FRY and ROAST, supported by at least three shRNAs
  depleted on their own, with no discordant shRNA;
* **Priority 2**: found by FRY and ROAST, but supported by fewer shRNAs;
* **Not recommended**: the call relies on discordant shRNAs (more
  discordant shRNAs than shRNAs depleted on their own).

Caveats that do not change the priority but must be kept in mind are listed
next to each gene.

```{r priority}
evidence <- evidence %>%
    mutate(
        Priority = factor(case_when(
            Discordant_shRNAs > Depleted_shRNAs ~ "Not recommended",
            FDR_FRY <= 0.05 & FDR_ROAST <= 0.05 & Depleted_shRNAs >= 3 &
                Discordant_shRNAs == 0 ~ "Priority 1",
            FDR_FRY <= 0.05 & FDR_ROAST <= 0.05 ~ "Priority 2",
            TRUE ~ "Not recommended"
        ), levels = c("Priority 1", "Priority 2", "Not recommended")),
        Caveats = paste0(
            ifelse(FDR_without_T4_TRT_1 > 0.05,
                "depends on T4_TRT_1; ", ""),
            ifelse(FDR_fitness_CTRL <= 0.05,
                "also lost in the controls (fitness); ", ""),
            ifelse(P_interaction > 0.05, "no clear increase from T3; ", ""),
            ifelse(Depleted_shRNAs < 3,
                paste(Depleted_shRNAs, "shRNA(s) depleted on their own; "),
                "")
        ),
        Caveats = sub("; $", "", Caveats)
    ) %>%
    arrange(Priority, FDR_FRY, Log2FC_T4)
evidence %>%
    select(Gene, Priority, Log2FC_T3, Log2FC_T4, FDR_FRY, FDR_ROAST,
        FDR_CAMERA, Depleted_shRNAs, shRNAs, Discordant_shRNAs,
        FDR_without_T4_TRT_1, P_interaction) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

# Hits to validate

```{r validate}
to_validate <- filter(evidence, Priority == "Priority 1")
also_consider <- filter(evidence, Priority == "Priority 2")
evidence %>%
    select(Gene, Priority, Log2FC_T4, FDR_FRY, Caveats) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

**The hits that should be validated first are
`r paste(to_validate$Gene, collapse = ", ")`.** They are depleted in the
treated cultures compared with the controls at T4 by the two self-contained
tests at 5% FDR, with median log2 fold changes between
`r round(min(to_validate$Log2FC_T4), 2)` and
`r round(max(to_validate$Log2FC_T4), 2)`, and each of them is supported by at
least three shRNAs depleted on their own and by no discordant shRNA. Their
caveats are in the table: a gene that is also lost in the controls is a
treatment-enhanced loss of fitness rather than a new dependency created by the
treatment, and a gene that depends on T4_TRT_1 should be confirmed in a new
experiment before anything else. `r paste(to_validate$Gene[to_validate$Caveats == ""], collapse = ", ")`
has no caveat: it is the most robust candidate of the screen.

`r paste(also_consider$Gene, collapse = ", ")` are also depleted at T4 by both
tests, but fewer of their shRNAs support them: they are second-line
candidates. Genes marked "Not recommended" rely on shRNAs that behave unlike
the others of the gene.

None of these genes is depleted at T3: these are **late treatment effects**,
which validation experiments should measure at the later time point.

## The hits at T3 and at T4

The normalized counts of the shRNAs of the hits to validate in the control and
treated cultures of the two time points show the treatment effect directly:
at T4 the treated cultures have lower counts than the controls, while at T3
the difference is small (the gene with a caveat on the time trend is the one
already slightly lower at T3). The shRNAs of a gene have very different
abundances, so each box spans a wide range: the comparison is between treated
and control samples of the same time point.

```{r validate-boxplots, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9}
plot_boxplot(object, genes = to_validate$Gene,
    group_var = c("CTRL", "TRT"), fill_var = "Treatment",
    ncol = nrow(to_validate)) +
    scale_y_continuous(transform = "log1p",
        breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 10000)) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 60))
```

`plot_barcode_trend()` follows each shRNA from T3 to T4 (log2 fold change of
treated vs control). In each gene several shRNAs go from no effect at T3 to a
depletion at T4:

```{r validate-barcode-trend, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 10}
plot_barcode_trend(metrics, genes = to_validate$Gene,
    n_col = nrow(to_validate))
```

`plot_barcode_hit()` places the shRNAs of a gene among all the barcodes of the
library, ranked by their log2 fold change. For the first hit to validate, at
T3 and at T4:

```{r validate-barcode-hit, fig.height = 5}
top_hit <- to_validate$Gene[1]
plot_barcode_hit(object, design, contrasts$T3, gene = top_hit) +
    plot_annotation(caption = "Treated vs control at T3")
plot_barcode_hit(object, design, contrasts$T4, gene = top_hit) +
    plot_annotation(caption = "Treated vs control at T4")
```

At T3 the shRNAs of the gene are spread over the ranking; at T4 several of
them are among the most depleted barcodes of the library.

Over the whole screen, the trend lines (mean normalized count of the shRNAs
of each gene) separate the hits to validate from an essential gene: the
essential gene is lost in control and treated cultures alike, while the hits
end lower in the treated cultures at T4.

```{r validate-trends, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 10}
top_essential <- essential$Gene[1]
trend <- function(condition) {
    plot_trend(object, genes = c(to_validate$Gene, top_essential),
        group_var = c("Infected", "Baseline", condition),
        ncol = nrow(to_validate) + 1) +
        ggtitle(condition)
}
trend("CTRL") / trend("TRT")
```

# Conclusions

* The screen is of good quality: deep sequencing, no bottleneck at infection
  or selection, and consistent replicates. The treated replicates at T4 are
  heterogeneous (T4_TRT_1 is close to the controls): without it the T4 hits
  are weaker, most of them just above 5% FDR, so their strength depends on
  this replicate.
* The strongest depletion in the screen is a **loss of fitness** shared by
  control and treated cultures: `r nrow(essential)` genes behave like
  essential genes and are not treatment hits.
* **Treatment-specific depletion appears at T4**, not at T3:
  `r nrow(hits_t4)` genes are depleted in treated compared with control
  cultures at T4 by the self-contained tests (5% FDR), with moderate effects;
  no gene is depleted at T3, and none at both time points.
* **Hits to validate: `r paste(to_validate$Gene, collapse = ", ")`**, with
  `r paste(also_consider$Gene, collapse = ", ")` as second-line candidates.
  They should be validated as late effects of the treatment (at the later
  time point), with individual shRNAs or other reagents against the same
  genes; the competitive tests do not single them out, so independent
  confirmation is essential.

# Limitations {#limitations}

The analysis above uses only methods whose statistical formulation fits the
question. Some questions of a longitudinal design are not fully covered by
ScreenR at present:

* **No built-in test of reproducibility across time points.** The
  intersection-union test is computed here from the per-time-point results;
  ScreenR has no function that does it, or that classifies genes as above.
* **No equivalence test.** ScreenR can show that a treatment effect changes
  over time (interaction), but not that it is the same at two time points:
  that needs an equivalence test with a margin chosen by the user.
* **Time as equally spaced steps.** `find_time_hit()` treats the time points
  as equally spaced and tests a linear change of the treatment effect; with
  two time points this is the interaction, with more it assumes linearity.
* **Gene-level effect sizes without uncertainty.** The gene log2 fold change
  is the median over its shRNAs, reported without a confidence interval.
* **Independent replicates.** The model treats the replicates of different
  time points as independent cultures. If replicate 1 at T3 and replicate 1
  at T4 come from the same culture, a design with the culture as a blocking
  factor would be more appropriate; the edgeR/limma based functions accept
  any design matrix, but `create_design_matrix()` does not build it.
* **Single-sample references.** T0 and the baseline have one sample each, so
  the fitness contrasts rely on the variability estimated from the
  replicated groups.
* **Multiplicity across questions.** The FDR is controlled within each
  contrast, not over all the contrasts together.
